name: Sumerian
era: c. 2600 – 1700 BC (Old Sumerian to Old Babylonian)
blurb: One of the first languages ever written, pressed into clay by the scribes of Ur, Uruk and Lagash.
facts: Sumerian is a language isolate: no relative of it has ever been found.
Cuneiform means 'wedge-shaped'. Scribes pressed the cut end of a reed into wet clay.
Sumerian died out as an everyday language around 2000–1800 BC, but scribes kept copying it for nearly two thousand years more, much as Europe kept Latin.
Students learned it in the e₂-dub-ba-a, the 'tablet house'. Their practice tablets, mistakes and all, still survive.
The sign 𒀭 began as a picture of a star. It reads an 'sky' and diĝir 'god'.
Sumerians called their country ki-en-gi and themselves saĝ gig₂-ga, 'the black-headed people'.

guide.p: Sumerian has no word for 'the' or 'a', and nouns are neither masculine nor feminine.
The adjective comes after its noun. lugal itself is lu₂ 'man' + gal 'big': the big man.
Add -e-ne to a word for people to make it plural. Things and animals stay as they are.
Each hyphenated piece is one cuneiform sign. Small numbers tell apart signs that sound alike: du 'go' and du₃ 'build' are different signs.

items.note: Often written dingir. The sign began as a star.
Borrowed from Akkadian. Older texts simply list things side by side.

units.title: Iri
units.about: City, temple and land, and saying what is

guide.p: e₂ is any house, and a god's house is a temple. e₂-gal, the 'big house', is the palace.
Put -am₃ on the end of what something is. It comes last, after the adjective.
kalam 'the Land' was Sumer seen from inside. kur, the mountains around the flat plain, meant foreign country. kur gal, 'Great Mountain', is a title of the god Enlil.
A sign can stand for several words. -am₃ is written with two signs, A and AN, and 𒀭 alone is both diĝir 'god' and an 'sky'.

items.note: On its own it can also mean silver.

units.title: Ĝe₂₆-e
units.about: My, your, and saying who you are

guide.p: -ĝu₁₀ 'my', -zu 'your' and -a-ni 'his, her' close the noun chain, after any adjective.
After a vowel -a-ni usually shrinks to -ni. e₂ 'house' keeps the a.
-am₃ is only 'he, she or it is'. For 'I am' and 'you are' use -me-en. The pronoun can be left out.

units.title: E₂ lugal-la
units.about: The king's house, the god's city

guide.p: The owner comes second and takes -ak: e₂ lugal-ak, 'house of the king'.
At the end of a phrase the k drops, and the a is written with a sign that repeats the owner's last consonant.
After a vowel the genitive often disappears from writing. Ur-Namma's bricks call him lugal ki-en-gi ki-uri, 'king of Sumer and Akkad'.
Gods' names start with a silent 𒀭 and cities end with a silent 𒆠. Scribes wrote them as labels; you do not type them.

items.note: The north, where Akkadian was spoken.
Goddess of love and war. Scholars spell her inana.
God of fresh water and cunning, 'Lord Earth'.
'House of heaven', Inanna's temple at Uruk. an 'heaven' + -ak.
nam- turns a noun into an idea: king, kingship.
Doubling a noun means 'all of them'.

units.title: Mu-na-du₃
units.about: Building, giving and who did it

guide.p: When a verb has an object, the one doing it takes -e. Someone who only stands or goes takes nothing.
The order is doer, object, verb. The plain form tells of something done, so in-du₃ is 'he built'.
The root comes last, with small prefixes before it. In in-du₃ the n means 'he or she did it'. -na- means 'for him' or 'to her'.
The person something is given to or done for takes -ra, and the verb repeats it with -na-.
ex: he built a house for the king

items.note: Written with the sign for a peg.

units.title: Mu-sar-ra
units.about: Lines that kings and scribes really wrote

guide.p: Ur-Namma of Ur (c. 2112–2095 BC) called himself nitaḫ kalag-ga 'mighty man', king of Ur, king of Sumer and Akkad. Other bricks add lu₂ e₂ en-lil₂-la₂ in-du₃-a: the -a turns 'he built' into 'who built'. Source: RIME 3/2.1.1.
Šulgi Hymn A opens lugal-me-en šag₄-ta ur-saĝ-me-en. -ta means 'from'. Šulgi also styled himself lugal an ub-da limmu₂-ba, 'king of the four quarters' of the world.
Letters open lugal-ĝu₁₀-ra u₃-na-a-dug₄, 'say to my king', because a messenger read them aloud (Royal Correspondence of Ur, ETCSL 3.1.01).

ud re-a ud su₃-ra₂ re-a opens the Instructions of Šuruppag and Gilgameš, Enkidu and the Netherworld. The Instructions go on with dumu-ĝu₁₀ na ga-de₅ (line 9; ga- is 'let me') and na de₅ ab-ba niĝ₂ kal-la-am₃ (line 13). kal-la 'precious' is the same sign as kalag.
Proverb Collection 2.47 (ETCSL 6.1.02) mocks a scribe who does not know eme-gi₇, Sumerian. nu- means 'not'.

items.note: One word written with two signs, ŠEŠ and AB, plus silent 𒆠.

units.title: I₃-du₃-e
units.about: Did or does: the two verb stems

guide.p: Every verb has a ḫamṭu stem for an action seen as done and whole, usually past, and a marû stem for an action still going on or still to come. Babylonian teachers called them 'quick' and 'slow' in Akkadian, and 'short' and 'long' in Sumerian, because marû forms are often longer.

guide.h: The doer moves to the end
guide.p: In ḫamṭu the doer is the n prefix. In marû it moves to the end as -e, and the verb opens with the plain prefix i₃-. The noun doing it still takes -e in both.
ex: the king will build the house

guide.p: Some verbs double instead: ĝar 'place' becomes ĝa₂-ĝa₂, and naĝ 'drink' becomes na₈-na₈, the same sign read na₈. A few swap roots: ĝen 'go' has the marû stem du, and dug₄ 'say' has e.
A verb without an object, like ĝen 'go', has no doer marker in either stem. Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1, line 63) says simply en-lil₂ i₃-ĝen, 'Enlil went'.
Sumerian marks aspect, not tense. A marû verb can mean 'is doing', 'does' or 'will do', and the story around it decides.

units.title: E-ne-ne
units.about: We, they, and verbs for many

guide.p: e-ne is 'he' or 'she' and e-ne-ne 'they', for people only. The verb already shows who acts, so pronouns are mostly for emphasis, and they never add the doer's -e.

The plural of 'to be' is -me-en-de₃-en 'we are', -me-en-ze₂-en 'you are' and -me-eš 'they are'. 'We' and 'you all' are just the first two standing alone. A proverb (ETCSL 6.1.08) begins ĝe₂₆-e u₃ za-e šeš-me-en-de₃-en.
In ḫamṭu a plural doer adds -eš at the end, written -uš after u, and keeps the n prefix. In the singular that n is often not written.
In marû the plural doer is the ending -ene, often written -ne. Enki's Journey to Nibru (ETCSL 1.1.4, line 110) has lu₂-e-ne kaš i₃-na₈-na₈-ne, 'they are drinking beer'.
-a-ne-ne is 'their' for people. -bi is 'its' or 'their' for things and animals, and it can also mean 'that'.

units.title: Udu
units.about: Numbers, sheep and silver in the temple economy

guide.p: Sumerians counted in tens and sixties. An upright wedge 𒁹 is one, a corner wedge 𒌋 is ten, and a bigger upright wedge 𒐕 is sixty. Our 60 minutes and 360 degrees go back to this Mesopotamian system.

Babylonian word lists give the spoken names: diš 1, min 2, eš₅ 3, limmu 4, ia₂ 5, aš₃ 6, imin 7, ussu 8, ilimmu 9, u 10, ĝeš₂ 60. Some readings are uncertain, so editions of accounts write the wedges instead.
Tablets write the number in wedges before the noun. Editions spell it as count and wedge: 5(diš) is five DIŠ wedges, 1(u) one ten. Literary editions often use plain digits instead.

Barley was measured in sila₃, about a litre; in Ur III 300 sila₃ made one gur. Silver was weighed in gin₂ 'shekels' of about 8 grams, and 60 shekels made a ma-na 'mina'. A messenger's ration list (ABTR 15, CDLI P100203) gives 5(diš) sila₃ kaš 5(diš) sila₃ ninda.
Add -kam, the genitive plus 'is', to a number to make an ordinal: ud 2(diš)-kam 'the second day'. Receipts date themselves this way.
The Sumerian King List (ETCSL 2.1.1) gives each reign as mu N i₃-ak, 'he made N years'. Its early kings rule for thousands of years; Gilgameš gets 126.

items.note: A measure of about one litre.

units.title: Ba-ḫul
units.about: More verb prefixes, and saying no

guide.p: ba- often marks something that happens to the subject with no doer named, much like an English passive. Ur III years were named after such events.
i₃- is the most neutral opening for a verb. Livestock receipts end with i₃-dab₅, 'he took charge'.
ḫe₂- (ḫa- before a) makes a wish or a firm statement. Letters to the kings of Ur often close with lugal-ĝu₁₀ ḫe₂-en-zu, 'may my king know it'. ḫe₂-ĝal₂, 'may there be', became the word for abundance.
nu- negates a verb and merges with the next prefix: nu + in-gu₇ is written nu-un-gu₇, 'he did not eat'. Before ba- it becomes la-.
ex: the king did not eat bread

guide.p: A receipt says what, from whom and who took it. ki X-ta is 'from X', literally 'from the place of X'. šu ba-ti, 'he received', joins šu 'hand' and ti 'come near'.

units.title: Diĝir-re-e-ne
units.about: Gods and myth, and chains of 'of'

guide.p: An, the sky, was king of the gods. His son Enlil ruled the earth from the Ekur at Nippur. Enki lived in the Abzu, the sweet water under the earth, at Eridu. Nanna the moon god was Enlil's firstborn and Inana's father.
One 'of' phrase can sit inside another. The genitives pile up at the end of the chain, so -ak + -ak after lugal is written -la-ka.
ex: the house of the king's son

guide.p: When an 'of' phrase does the action, -ak and the doer's -e merge into -ke₄, as in Ur-Namma's bricks: lugal urim₅-ma-ke₄.
ex: the king of the land built the house

guide.p: After a vowel the genitive often vanishes from writing, so 'An, king of the gods' is just an lugal diĝir-re-e-ne. diĝir-re-e-ne is diĝir + -e-ne, with the r written again.
me are the divine powers that make civilisation work: kingship, priesthood, the crafts, the scribal art. In one myth Inana gets Enki drunk and carries them off from Eridu to Uruk (ETCSL 1.3.1).

units.title: Gilgameš
units.about: Proverbs, hymns and the Gilgameš poems

guide.p: Five Sumerian poems tell of Gilgameš, lord of Kulaba in Uruk. They survive in Old Babylonian school copies, and later poets reworked them into the Akkadian Epic of Gilgameš. ETCSL writes his name gilgameš₂; ePSD2 reads the same signs as Bilgames.
ga- on a ḫamṭu verb means 'let me' or 'I will'. In Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa he tells Enkidu kur-ra ga-an-kur₉ mu-ĝu₁₀ ga-am₃-ĝar (ETCSL 1.8.1.5, line 5).
ex: let me set up my name

guide.p: -gin₇ makes a simile. Enheduana sings to Inana ušumgal-gin₇ kur-re uš₁₁ ba-e-šum₂, 'like a dragon you have deposited venom on the foreign lands' (ETCSL 4.07.2, line 9).
In ḫamṭu an -e- before the root means 'you did it': ba-e-šum₂ 'you gave', mu-e-il₂ 'you raised'.
Poetry repeats a line with one change. The Flood story has ud 7-am₃ ĝi₆ 7-am₃, 'seven days, seven nights' (ETCSL 1.7.4, segment D, line 3). The -am₃ means 'it is': 'it was seven'.
Hymns end with a name and za₃-mi₂, 'praise'. Many school texts close with nisaba za₃-mi₂, 'praise be to Nisaba', the goddess of writing.
-še₃ means 'toward'. A verb can describe a noun: e₂ an-ta ed₃-de₃ is 'the house coming down from heaven'. na- on the opening verb of a poem often marks a story being told.

items.note: Gilgameš's servant in the Sumerian poems, his friend in the later epic.
